changelog.note: Fitted to the 24 calibration units, so those units are not a fair test of it; the blind preference test is the hold-out. Session counts are not numbers for honest_numbers; a [planted] tag makes honest_numbers N/A; a concrete case must be one you can picture and may sit in the notes; evidence slides skip visual, delight, concrete_first and guess_reveal; a detail slide scores on what it adds to an overview; several findings behind one claim are one idea. Clear wording allows playful language, short punchy lines and images in words that have a reasonable reading; undefined jargon still counts against it.

Fitted to the 24 calibration units and Andrew's round-two rulings, so those units are not a fair test of it; the blind preference test is the hold-out. Each unit now carries the base criteria plus one device: guess_reveal and delight are retired as per-unit criteria and replaced by device, which names the device type, and the arc gains variety, which checks that the types vary across the deck. New base criterion economy (no filler on the unit) with a short list of filler patterns check.py gates on slide text. New deck criterion notes_actionable (every instruction in the notes names the exact move and defines what it refers to). Flow gains a 4 anchor: a topic change the narrative supports. An exercise with no fixed answer is not a failed guess before reveal; it scores on its own device. The arc keeps flow, delight and participation; arc flow now accepts a supported topic change.

Two lessons from the A4 blind preference notes. Visual: a recurring character or mascot used as decoration, or an image whose metaphor is unclear or does not fit the slide, scores at most 3. Clear: violent wording about an idea, such as "kill", reads as violent or about people; it is a clear-criterion note and not a banned term, because check.py applies banned terms to speaker notes as well as slide text.

Fitted to the 17 notes from the A4 blind preference test, where both graders scored clear and visual 4 or 5 on slides the reader faulted, so those slides are not a fair test of it. Clear becomes a cold-reader test: the grader first writes the point a first-time audience member would take and lists every word, name, label, title or question that person would have to guess at; 5 needs an empty list and a title that states the point, one guess caps it at 3, two or more give 1. Visual judges whether the visual works: every colour, position, order and grouping must mean something the slide or its notes make clear, and the visual must be complete; an unexplained colour, a broken encoding, an incomplete visual, a decorative mascot or an unclear metaphor caps it at 3. Economy: a text-heavy slide whose narrative could live in the speaker notes scores at most 3, and a list longer than the idea needs counts as filler. prefer_rulings.py turns every preference test's notes into rulings.

scale.na: N/A needs a reason, like a score does. N/A outside na_allowed fails schema validation.

na_conditions.first_unit: The unit is the first unit of the draft.
na_conditions.no_number: The unit contains no number, or its only numbers describe the session or the draft itself: timings such as "90 minutes", positions such as "Exercise 3 of 4", counts of its own acts, parts, questions or clusters, and labels such as C1 to C9 or D1. A unit with digits may be N/A on this ground; the reason says the numbers describe the session.
na_conditions.planted: The unit is marked planted: its speaker notes carry a [planted] tag because it holds a deliberately fabricated figure, planted as a teaching trick. It must be N/A.
na_conditions.no_notes: The unit has no speaker notes. It must be N/A.

criteria.name: Highly visual
criteria.question: Does the visual work: does a chart, infographic, cartoon or shape carry the idea, does every colour, position, order and grouping in it mean something the slide or its notes make clear, is it complete, and does the slide look different from the one before it?

anchors.1: Text only, or the only image is a logo or a small icon. The slide looks the same as the one before it.
anchors.3: A visual is present but does not fully work. Any one of these caps visual at 3: it decorates the words rather than carrying the idea; a colour difference the slide and notes never explain (two regions coloured red among neutral ones, with no reason given); a broken encoding (a funnel whose stages do not narrow, an arrow where a tick is meant); an incomplete visual (part of a ladder, list or diagram the idea needs is cut off or missing, such as three of four rungs); items that belong together not grouped visibly; a recurring character or mascot used as decoration; an image whose metaphor is unclear or does not fit the slide; or the slide repeats the previous slide's look.
anchors.5: A chart, infographic, cartoon or shape carries the idea, every colour, position, order and grouping means something the slide or its notes make clear, nothing the idea needs is cut off or missing, items that belong together are grouped visibly, and the slide looks different from the one before it. A logo or a small icon does not count. A mascot counts only when it acts out the slide's idea and its metaphor is clear.

criteria.name: Clear wording
criteria.question: Would a first-time audience member take the slide's point without guessing? Before scoring, write in "point" the one sentence that person would take from the unit, and list in "guesses" every word, name, label, title or question they would have to guess at: a step name that does not say what the step is, a subtitle whose purpose is unclear, a question the audience cannot parse, quadrant or axis labels the unit never explains, an ordering label that does not fit the order, undefined jargon. Playful language, a short punchy line or an image in words is not a guess when it has a reasonable reading.

anchors.1: Two or more guesses, or the point cannot be paraphrased ("point" is empty).
anchors.3: Exactly one guess. Violent wording about an idea, such as "kill" or "die", counts as one guess: it reads as violent or about people, so say what happens to the idea (it stops, it is dropped).
anchors.5: No guesses, and the title states the point plainly. Playful language, a short punchy line or an image in words is fine when it has a reasonable reading.

criteria.name: Flow
criteria.question: Is the logic step from the previous unit to this one obvious without the speaker?

anchors.1: No visible link to the previous unit. The step needs the speaker, or the unit is out of order.
anchors.3: The link exists but the reader has to work it out, or it depends on a line only the speaker says.
anchors.4: A change of topic that the narrative supports: the reader sees why the draft moves on, though the step is not the obvious next one.
anchors.5: A logic step from the previous unit to this one is obvious without the speaker.

criteria.name: One device
criteria.question: Besides the base criteria, does the unit carry exactly one device, a trick or twist that involves the audience, without giving an answer away before its moment? Name the device type.

anchors.1: No device: a flat statement with nothing for the audience to predict, do or feel, or a preview that gives an answer away before its moment. A recurring character used as decoration is not a device.
anchors.3: A device is present but weak (a predictable payoff, a small spoiler), or two devices compete for the same unit.
anchors.5: One clear device carries the unit. A surprising, insightful rule stated plainly counts. An exercise with no fixed answer is not a failed guess before reveal: it scores on its own device, usually a live challenge.

types.guess_reveal: Guess before reveal: the audience predicts before the answer lands, judged on this unit with the one before. A prediction that is possible but not invited, or a previous unit that half gives the answer away, is weak.
types.surprise: A surprise: the audience is teased or tricked, and the unit is part of a journey rather than a preview. A map of the session's shape is fine; giving an answer away before its moment is not.
types.tease_payoff: A tease paid off later: a tagged hook ([hook:x]) that a later unit pays off ([payoff:x]), or the payoff of an earlier hook.
types.callback: A callback: an earlier idea or a recurring character returns where it helps, never as decoration.
types.live_challenge: A live challenge: the audience does something now, such as placing their own work, answering out loud or arguing a case.
types.overturn: An insight that overturns an assumption the audience holds.
types.plain_rule: A surprising, insightful rule stated plainly.
types.none: No device. Use it with a score of 1 and with N/A.

criteria.name: One idea per unit
criteria.question: Does the unit carry exactly one idea?

anchors.1: Three or more ideas compete, or there is no idea at all.
anchors.3: One main idea with a second idea that pulls attention away from it, such as a finding that points somewhere the main claim does not.
anchors.5: One idea per slide, or per section part. Several studies or findings that all support one claim are one idea.

criteria.name: Concrete before abstract
criteria.question: Does an example or case come before the principle?

anchors.1: The principle comes alone, with no case you can picture anywhere. A rule, a test or a thesis sentence is still the principle, never the example.
anchors.3: A case is present but comes after the principle, or is too general to picture: no named organisation, event, person or figure.
anchors.5: A case you can picture (a named organisation, event, person or figure) comes before the principle. The case may sit in the speaker notes, so a slide needs no forced story moment.

criteria.name: Economy
criteria.question: Does every word, sentence and element on the unit serve its core message? Judge the slide's visible text and elements, or the article text; speaker notes are not judged here. A piece of filler is one sentence, phrase or element that does not serve the core message: meta-commentary that counts or describes what is visible ("nine rules on the page", "all nine"), an instruction on how to consume the unit ("Do not read all nine out"), the "not X, but Y" or "it's this, not that" pattern, a line added for completeness rather than meaning, or list items beyond what the idea needs (four questions where three carry the idea). A text-heavy slide whose narrative could live in the speaker notes scores at most 3, however tight each sentence is.

anchors.1: Two or more pieces of filler.
anchors.3: One piece of filler, or a text-heavy slide whose narrative could move to the speaker notes.
anchors.5: No filler: cutting any word, sentence or element would weaken the core message.

criteria.name: Earns its place
criteria.question: Would cutting this unit lose something?

anchors.1: A unit that repeats a neighbour. Cutting it loses nothing.
anchors.3: It adds something, but a neighbour could absorb it with one sentence. Repeating an earlier overview's items is not by itself a reason for 3.
anchors.5: Cutting it would lose something the draft needs. A detail slide scores on what it adds that an earlier overview lacks: a test, a condition or an action.

criteria.name: Honest numbers
criteria.question: Does every number carry its source and its limit?

anchors.1: A number with no source and no limit. Counts that describe the session itself (timings, exercise positions, counts of acts or clusters, labels like C1 to C9) are not numbers here.
anchors.3: Every number has a source, but a limit is missing, or the source is vague.
anchors.5: Every number has its source and its limit, on the slide, in the notes, or in the article's references. A unit whose only numbers describe the session is N/A, never 5.

criteria.name: Actionable notes
criteria.question: Does every instruction in the speaker notes name the exact move and define what it refers to? "Ask them for the forbidden list out loud" fails, because the notes never say which list; "Ask the room for an agentic opportunity, then ask what is forbidden in that example" passes. Notes with no instruction score on whether every reference they make is defined.

anchors.1: Two or more instructions a presenter could not carry out as written: the move is vague, or it refers to something the notes never define.
anchors.3: One instruction is vague or refers to something undefined; the rest name the exact move.
anchors.5: Every instruction names the exact move and defines what it refers to.

arc.inputs: Every unit's text and notes in order, the run sheet, and a contact sheet of all screenshots. One call per round per grader.

criteria.name: Flow
criteria.question: Does each unit follow from the one before, across the whole draft? A change of topic that the narrative supports counts as following.

criteria.name: Surprise and delight
criteria.question: Is the whole draft a journey that involves, teases or tricks the audience?

criteria.name: Participation
criteria.question: Is the audience involved often enough, judged against the run sheet's own act windows and exercise timings?

anchors.1: Long stretches with nothing for the audience to do, against the run sheet's own windows.
anchors.3: Involvement exists but clusters, leaving at least one act window passive.
anchors.5: Every act window involves the audience, at the timings the run sheet sets.

criteria.name: Device variety
criteria.question: Do the devices vary across the deck? Name each unit's device type (guess before reveal, surprise, tease paid off later, callback, live challenge, insight that overturns an assumption, surprising rule stated plainly).

anchors.1: One device type dominates the deck, or the same type repeats on consecutive units throughout.
anchors.3: Mostly varied, but the same type sits on two consecutive units, or one type covers more than half the units with a device.
anchors.5: The types vary: no two consecutive units share a type and no type covers more than half the units with a device.

arc.hook_payoff: Every [hook:<name>] tag in the notes has a matching [payoff:<name>] tag later.

banned_terms.why: Jargon, stays out of the room.
Ontology jargon, stays out of the room.
Ontology jargon, stays out of the room.
Jargon, stays out of the room.
Evidence-grading jargon, stays out of the room.
No call to action anywhere in a deck.

bars.split_regrade: Where one grader gives 3 and the other 4 or more, the lower grader re-grades that unit once and the second score stands.

filler_patterns.why: An instruction on how to consume the slide.
An instruction on how to consume the slide.
An instruction on how to consume the slide.
